case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: Feist protects facts, not the expressive text that carries them. It says little about verbatim reproduction, which is where the strongest claims against generative systems are actually pleaded.
case.holding: Facts are not copyrightable, however much labour went into collecting them. Only original selection, coordination and arrangement can be protected, and effort alone earns nothing.

case.why_ai_cites_it: It underwrites the argument that what a model extracts from a corpus is uncopyrightable fact and statistical relationship rather than protected expression, and it forecloses the sweat-of-the-brow theory that a dataset is owned because it was expensive to assemble.

reading.body:
Feist v. Rural Telephone, the 1991 case holding that facts are not copyrightable regardless of the effort spent collecting them, underwrites the defense argument that what a model extracts from training data is uncopyrightable fact and statistical relationship rather than protected expression.

It is quoted directly in the CNN v. Perplexity AI litigation and cited across the broader 79-case defense pool elsewhere in this collection, and its stated limit draws a specific line. Feist protects facts, not the expressive text that carries them, which the case record notes is exactly where the strongest claims against generative systems, verbatim reproduction, are actually pleaded.

The data does not say whether the CNN case turns on facts extracted or text reproduced specifically, only that Feist's fact-versus-expression line is the specific distinction the case record says the strongest claims turn on.
